fields.expected: I want to work on systems where performance and correctness are both non-negotiable, and a supercomputing software role is closer to that than anything I have done so far. Most of my work has been one level up the stack. At Summer Atlantic Capital I built the machine-learning core of an anomaly-detection system, including the event-ingestion pipeline, a versioned FastAPI microservice, the CI scaffold, and temporal sequence models over event streams. Doing that taught me that model quality is often not the constraint. Throughput, failure modes, and whether the infrastructure holds up under real load usually are. I want to go deeper on that layer rather than keep treating it as plumbing underneath the model. I also work best when I own a real piece of a system instead of isolated tickets, which is how I built ClarityAtlas end to end and shipped it into a Hopkins pilot with 30+ users. An on-site San Jose internship on hard software problems is exactly the environment I am looking for.

fields.expected:
- I built ClarityAtlas, an iOS health app, end to end in Swift/SwiftUI with Supabase, including a passive sleep-estimation system that infers sleep without a wearable using HealthKit and Core Motion signals like step count, gait speed, and movement patterns. We shipped it into a live Hopkins pilot with 30+ users, got selected for the Pava Spark Accelerator and NSF I-Corps, received a non-binding indication of about $75,000 for roughly 7-8% equity, and pitched Hopkins President Ron Daniels after knocking on the doors of Garland Hall until we got in.
- I was lead model developer on a Gates Foundation-funded Hopkins / South African Medical Research Council project, training XGBoost models on a national survey dataset of roughly 10 million records, using SHAP for feature selection and interpretation, and designing G-formula causal simulations to estimate counterfactual intervention outcomes.
- I did independent research on Valley Fever, building an SIR-style epidemiological model in Python from its differential equations and programming a microcontroller dust sensor in C/C++. It became a sole-author publication in the Journal of Student Research and a national finalist spot at the Junior Science and Humanities Symposium.

fields.expected:
Two things that did not fit elsewhere. First, the closest I have come to working near hardware is small but real: for my Valley Fever research I programmed a microcontroller-based dust sensor in C/C++ and built an SIR-style epidemiological model in Python from its differential equations, connecting disease dynamics to environmental variables. That work became a sole-author publication in the Journal of Student Research and a national finalist spot at the Junior Science and Humanities Symposium. I mention it because I like going down a level when the problem requires it rather than staying where I am already comfortable.

Second, I spend a lot of time on where automation should stop. In a Playwright-based job-application agent I built in TypeScript, every mutating capability sits behind fail-closed environment flags, and I built a validation ladder so a capability is not called working until it has been confirmed against the level of reality it claims to support, not just a local fixture. That habit, refusing to trust a green test that only proves something narrow, is what I would bring to systems work.
